content.rendered:
What a Way to Make a Living:
Envisioning the potential of NYC’s Block by Block affordable housing plan
Thursday, November 12, 6–8 pm
303 Bond Street, Brooklyn

​As New York City advances its Block-by-Block agenda to construct 400,000 new and renovated homes across the city, this gathering convenes leading voices across policy, design, and development. Together, we’ll examine critical policy gaps around sustainability, infrastructure, and public space, and explore how housing plans can move beyond unit production to foster better forms of living.

RSVP

Participants

  • ​Annie Barrett, aanda (Moderator)

  • ​Pamela Cabrera, Transsolar KlimaEngineering (Moderator)

  • ​Arielle Hersh, Urban Homesteading Assistance Board

  • ​Jenny French and Anda French, French 2D

  • ​Daniel Roche, The Architect’s Newspaper

  • ​Susanne Schindler, Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies

  • ​Iziah Thompson, Community Service Society of New York

​This event is presented by the Van Alen Vanguard, a dynamic network of emerging design leaders. Annie Barrett and Pamela Cabrera are among the inaugural cohort developing public programs and exhibitions that reimagine designers’ roles in civic life and center equity, resilience, and local knowledge.

title.rendered: Re-Forming the Image: A Collage Walk with Curry J. Hackett

content.rendered:
Re-Forming the Image: A Collage Walk
Saturday, October 10, 1–3 pm
303 Bond Street, Brooklyn

 

Free with RSVP

 

Presented by the Ace Hotel Brooklyn, join this architectural walk and collage workshop with multimedia artist, educator and current 2026 Artist-in-Residence Curry J. Hackett.

 

Guests will learn to tell stories by remix archival images, photos, and ephemera from the artist-in-residence to develop their own reimaginings of Gowanus and Downtown Brooklyn. The walk will begin at Van Alen Institute and culminate at Ace Hotel Brooklyn for a brief discussion on the work. Using collage as a method, guests will then put the methods that Hackett employed in the residency to create speculative stories of the land observed along the walk.

 

Curry J. Hackett is among the inaugural cohort of the Van Alen Vanguard, a dynamic network of emerging design leaders developing public programs and exhibitions that reimagine designers’ roles in civic life.

 

Please note this is a 0.6 mile walking tour along paved, but sometimes uneven sidewalks.

 

What’s included:

All collage material included printed matter, scissors, glue, paper

 

What to bring:

Comfortable walking shoes
Weather appropriate clothing
Water bottle

content.rendered:
Open Access: Exploring 130 Years of American Design
Exhibition Reception
Thursday, October 8, 6–8 pm
303 Bond Street, Brooklyn

 

Free with RSVP

 

On view October 8–November 13 at Van Alen Institute, Open Access: Exploring 130 Years of American Design invites five artists and design teams to respond to our archive. Comprising thousands of competition boards, jury records, photographs, and correspondence, it’s one of the most significant collections of American architectural history in existence.

 

But an archive is never neutral. It reflects the priorities, blind spots, and values of those who built it: who was invited in, whose ideas were resourced, and whose were left out entirely. In Open Access, each project asks a different version of the same question: what does this archive tell us about who design has — and hasn’t — served?

 

On October 8, join us for a festive cocktail reception, take a first look at the exhibition, and toast the exhibiting artists: Annie Barrett, Daniel Pittman, and Paula Vilaplana de Miguel; Kholisile Dhliwayo; Friends Making Work; PROPS SUPPLY; and Gillian Waldo.

content.rendered:
Culture of Place: A conversation with Farida Abu-Bakare (WXY), Curry J. Hackett, and Tura Cousins Wilson (SOCA)
Thursday, November 5, 6–8 pm
303 Bond Street, Brooklyn

 

Free with RSVP

 

A neighborhood’s future depends in part on the organizations that give people a place to gather and a voice in what happens next. How can architecture support that work? Join architect Farida Abu-Bakare in conversation with designer, artist, and educator Curry J. Hackett, and architect Tura Cousins Wilson of Studio of Contemporary Architecture (SOCA) to explore how community organizations can shape stronger, more connected neighborhoods.

 

Drawing on the participants’ respective practices, the discussion will consider how design can sustain local cultural life while responding to changing community needs. The participants bring distinct perspectives on Black cultural memory and the relationships between communities and the spaces they inhabit. Together, they will examine what architects can learn from the people already doing the work of building community, and how those relationships can give residents a greater role in shaping the places they call home.

 

This event is presented by the Van Alen Vanguard, a dynamic network of emerging design leaders. Farida Abu-Bakare and Curry J. Hackett are among the inaugural cohort developing public programs and exhibitions that reimagine designers’ roles in civic life and center equity, resilience, and local knowledge.

title.rendered: The Architectural Anarchive: Reimagining the Design Archive

content.rendered:
The Architectural Anarchive: Reimagining the Design Archive
Monday, October 19, 6–8pm
303 Bond Street, Brooklyn

RSVP

Presented alongside our fall exhibition Open Access: Exploring 130 Years of American Design, Shannon Mattern leads a panel discussion with Dorothy Berry, Karilyn Crockett, M.C. Overholt, and Olga Touloumi. Together they’ll draw inspiration from the elusive concept of “anarchitecture” — characterized variously by the cut and the collective, absence and activation, excess and erasure.

We’ll assess and reimagine the architectural “an-archive” as a site where knowledge workers, scholars, designers, planners, students, and community members converge.

​How do (or could) archives condition what constitutes architecture, what’s worthy of collection and preservation, who counts among its stakeholders, what records or artifacts document its existence, and what alternative worlds might be conceivable?

Given the exhibition’s focus on “open and fair access,” we’ll consider what those concepts mean for an architectural archive in an age when extractive, surveillant technologies and authoritarian regimes have threatened knowledge infrastructures and public architectures.

Event Schedule

6 pm: Doors open
6:30 pm: Conversation
7:30 pm: Reception

About Shannon Mattern

Shannon Mattern is the Director of Creative Research at the Metropolitan New York Library Council. Previously, she held full professorships in media studies, anthropology, and art history at The New School and the University of Pennsylvania. Her research and teaching focus on media architectures, information infrastructures, and urban technologies. She is the author of The New Downtown Library: Designing with Communities; Deep Mapping the Media City; Code and Clay, Data and Dirt: 5000 Years of Urban Media; and A City Is Not a Computer. She also contributes a regular long-form column about urban data and mediated infrastructures to Places Journal and regularly collaborates on public design and interactive projects and exhibitions. You can find her at wordsinspace.net.

title.rendered: The Accidental Archive: A Community Workshop

content.rendered:
The Accidental Archive: A Community Workshop
Thursday, October 22, 6–8 pm
303 Bond Street, Brooklyn

Presented alongside our fall exhibition Open Access: Exploring 130 Years of American Design, join this interactive workshop led by writer and artist Divya Mehra. We’ll glean through our own personal archives and ask questions about value, the mundane, and what it means to choose to embrace our own archival practice.

Participants will bring an accumulation of their own — digital or physical — and translate it into a personal archive. Using a series of constraints inspired by Oulipo and other rule-based approaches (sorting, removing, repeating, obscuring, connecting, rearranging) we’ll treat these fragments as material. Through language, drawing, collage, and classification, individual records will gradually become a physical archive assembled from the things we happened to keep. What patterns emerge when we reorganize the everyday? What do the things we carry tell us about ourselves?

An Archival Séance: The Critical Record with Marina Otero Verzier
Thursday, October 29, 6–8 pm
303 Bond Street, Brooklyn

Presented alongside our fall exhibition Open Access: Exploring 130 Years of American Design, join us for a séance-inspired evening to interrogate the archival holdings unboxed in the show.

Exhibition participants will each present select materials from Van Alen’s archive through a performance of light and shadow. Moderator Marina Otero Verzier and respondent Mark Wasiuta, in conversation with the participating artists, will guide the audience through the hidden histories these materials represent and exclude. Together they will explore the topic of “the critical record:” How do scholars, historians, and critics actively reinterpret official architectural archives?

The evening’s séance format is informed by participating artist Paula Vilaplana de Miguel’s research exploring the performance of haunting as a critical tool in 19th century’s North American Spiritualist movement, and its spatial configuration — in particular, “the psychic cabinet,” an interpretation of which is part of the exhibition and will serve as the stage for the event.

About Marina Otero Verzier

Marina Otero Verzier is an architect and researcher whose work lies at the intersection of critical spatial practices, ecology, technology, and activism. She is a Lecturer in Architecture at Harvard GSD and a Dean’s Visiting Assistant Professor at Columbia University’s GSAPP, where she leads the Data Mourning clinic, an educational initiative examining the relationship between digital infrastructures and climate catastrophe.

About Mark Wasiuta

Mark Wasiuta is Co-Director of the Critical, Curatorial and Conceptual Practices in Architecture program at Columbia University’s GSAPP. He works on problems of media, environment, and technology in postwar architecture and its experimental practices. He is currently curating and producing Early Warning Architecture, the official representation for Canada at the 20th International Architecture Exhibition of the Venice Biennale.

title.rendered: Book Launch: Material Variance by Lola Ben-Alon

content.rendered:
Book Launch: Material Variance
Thursday, November 19, 6–8 pm
303 Bond Street, Brooklyn

Please join us for the unveiling of a site-specific work by Lola Ben-Alon’s Natural Materials Lab at Columbia GSAPP. Along with this installation, Lola will be debuting her new book Material Variance (Columbia Books on Architecture and the City). More details to be announced.

RSVP

​About Material Variance

Raw building materials are inherently variable. This variability shapes global supply chains, labor relations, infrastructure​, and trade networks. And yet, within the context of building design, materials are often treated as static commodities. Material Variance resists this perception, unfolding instead a framework for designing through and with living matter that is uncertain, messy, and dynamic. The book insists on materials not as passive inputs but as unruly agents, shaped by and shaping the political, ecological, and cultural processes around them.

Convening material researchers, building scientists, architects, and artists, Material Variance aims to collectively expand architecture and design’s material lexicon and unsettle its disciplinary boundaries. The book interrogates the assumptions of refinement, standardization, and technocratic control to advance alternative fabrication practices, alchemical processes, and methods for working with indeterminate matter. From poetic field recordings to scientific analyses, the book opens up a space for thinking across theory and practice, across geological particles and living species, and across various scales, forms, and practices.

This edition of Material Variance features three distinct covers, each one printed with a unique matrix, ink, paper stock, and tip-in, extending the notion of variance to production of the object itself.

With contributions from David Benjamin, Ethan Bordeau, Olga Beatrice Carcassi, Caitlin Charlet, Felecia Davis, Andrés Jaque, Leslie Lok, Mae-ling Lokko, Claudia Marais, Adam Marcus, V. Mitch McEwen, Ruth Morrow, Jorge Otero-Pailos, Ronald Rael, Jonsara Ruth, and Laia Mogas-Soldevila.

– cup.columbia.edu

title.rendered: Book Launch: Junior Architects

content.rendered:
​Book Launch: Junior Architects
Monday, November 9, 6–8 pm
303 Bond Street, Brooklyn

 

Free with RSVP

 

Please join us at Van Alen for a conversation hosted by Suzanne Lettieri and Anya Sirota, editors of Junior Architects: New Paradigms in Design Education (Park Books).

​

This new publication examines the pursuit of equity in architecture and design education in the United States amid widening political divides around race and class. Bringing together contributors to the book and leaders of local enrichment programs, the event will take stock of this work, its histories and its ambitions, and ask where it might go next. It is an opportunity to reconnect, reflect, and consider how more equitable pathways into architecture and design might continue to be built.

Event Schedule

​6 pm — Doors open
6:30 pm — Conversation and Q&A
7:15 pm — Reception
8 pm — Close

​Participants

  • ​Milton S. F. Curry is Professor of Architecture and Senior Associate Dean at Cornell University’s College of Architecture, Art, and Planning. His work focuses on urban development and cultural theory in the Americas.
  • Erin Pellegrino is a registered architect, strategist, and educator committed to transforming the architecture profession. She co-founded Out of Architecture, a career resource community and talent agency supporting architects transitioning beyond traditional practice, and co-authored Out of Architecture: The Value of Architects Beyond Traditional Practice.
  • Quilian Riano is Dean of Pratt Institute’s School of Architecture and Vice President for Architecture at the Architectural League of New York. He founded DSGN AGNC, a studio exploring cooperative design in architecture, urbanism, landscapes, and art.
RSVP

title.rendered: Book Talk: A Right to Housing? with Samuel Stein

content.rendered:
​Book Talk: A Right to Housing?
Wednesday, November 4, 6–8 pm
303 Bond Street, Brooklyn

 

Free with RSVP

 

Join the AIA Brooklyn Housing Committee for an evening with author Samuel Stein, in conversation with Andrew Brown, Director of Programs, Van Alen Institute, on the urgent question of housing as a right. Stein will introduce his new book A Right to Housing? and its untraditional structure with a short reading, followed by a discussion on the issues and questions the book raises — from the politics of housing policy to what a genuine right to housing could look like in practice. Copies of the book will be available for purchase at the event.

 

About A Right to Housing?

 

​In the fight for housing, we are caught between the world we know and the world we want. This book is both a road map and a reckoning. Drawing on his own experience of on-the-ground organizing, Samuel Stein presents practical policies for enacting a right to shelter, a right to a home, and a right to the city itself.

 

​With raw honesty, he then explores why these visions founder on the rocks of political reality. He reveals the forces blocking our path—from the power of real estate capital to the inadequacy of our institutions—and captures the complex feelings of a left that has lost faith in the future.

​

​— versobooks.com

title.rendered: Book Launch: At the Edge of Where God Built

content.rendered:
Book Launch: At the Edge of Where God Built
Tuesday, October 27, 6–8 pm
303 Bond Street, Brooklyn

 

Free with RSVP

 

​Celebrate the release of At the Edge of Where God Built, a new book from Actar Publishers by Ziad Jamaleddine & Makram el Kadi of L.E.FT Architects. A conversation with the authors will be moderated by Nader Tehrani of NADAAA.

 

​At the Edge of Where God Built undertakes a critical examination of L.E.FT Architects’ diverse body of work from the past decade, reorganizing their designs, research, and pedagogy around five key Arabic spatial terms: tawaf (circumambulation space), jami (mosque space), riwaq (a courtyard’s colonnade), dar (domestic space), and khirba (a ruin). Rooted in the Arab-speaking, Islamic geographies of the Middle East and North Africa, these terms illuminate and conceptualize L.E.FT’s investigations into forms of contemporary religious and non-religious architecture.

 

About L.E.FT

​L.E.FT was founded in New York in 2004. The office was a member of Architectural Record’s 2010 Design Vanguard for top firms in the United States, and was selected to the AD100, The Best Designers in the Middle East and North Africa (2025). L.E.FT’s work includes the Beirut Exhibition Center (2011), and Shakib Arslan Mosque, Lebanon (2017), winner of the Interfaith Design (AIA) & Partners of Sacred Places Award in Religious Architecture (2018), and the Al Fozan Award for Mosque Architecture (2022). L.E.FT recently completed the Office of Religious and Spiritual Life and Contemplative Practices, Vassar College (2023), winner of the Interfaith Design (AIA) & Partners of Sacred Places Award in Religious Architecture: Adaptive Re-Use (2024), and LOOP Design Awards: Religious & Spiritual (2024). The office’s research and design work has been exhibited at several cultural venues, including Oslo Architecture Triennale (2016), Milan Triennale (2019), Sharjah Architecture Triennale (2019), and Jeddah Islamic Arts Biennale (2023).

​About Nader Tehrani

​Nader Tehrani is an Iranian-American designer and educator who founded NADAAA in partnership with Katherine Faulkner in 2011. Working on interdisciplinary platforms, Nader Tehrani’s research has been focused on the transformation of the building industry, innovative material applications, and the development of new means and methods of construction.

title.rendered: They Have Watches but We Have Time: A Takeover by WAI Architecture Think Tank

content.rendered:
They Have Watches but We Have Time:
A Takeover by WAI Architecture Think Tank
Tuesday, October 13, 6–8 pm
303 Bond Street, Brooklyn

RSVP

​For one evening, WAI Architecture Think Tank transforms Van Alen Institute into a living postcolonial collage, inspired by the abolitionist Afro-Asian Bookstore of political prisoner Martin Sostre and the mutual-aid restaurants and loudreadings of anarcho-syndicalist and feminist Luisa Capetillo. Through books, artifacts, food, loudreadings, lectures, and performances, the evening questions whose histories the archive preserves alongside:

  • ​Nathalie Frankowski & Cruz Garcia with Ema Yuizarix, WAI Architecture Think Tank
  • ​Luis Othoniel Rosa, writer; Associate Professor of Spanish and Ethnic Studies, University of Nebraska–Lincoln
  • ​Rose Florian, architect and urban designer; Post-Novis
  • ​Daniel Jonas Roche, journalist; News Editor, The Architect’s Newspaper
  • ​Lane Rick, architect, artist, and educator; co-founder, Office of Things
  • ​Nora Akawi, architect and curator; Assistant Professor, The Cooper Union
  • ​Iskander Guetta & Quang Vinh Nguyen, designers and curators of the series

​The evening is part of They Have Watches but We Have Time, an exhibition and program conceived by Iskander Guetta and Quang Vinh Nguyen, Swiss designers and researchers in the Master of Environmental Design program at the Yale School of Architecture, in collaboration with the Consulate General of Switzerland in New York on the occasion of Archtober 2026. The project treats time as a material of design, asking how time is measured, organized, and imposed.

​About WAI Architecture Think Tank

​Founded in 2008 by Cruz Garcia and Nathalie Frankowski, WAI Architecture Think Tank is a planetary studio dedicated to critical spatial practices and alternative design education. Operating across Puerto Rico, France, and the USA, WAI also co-leads LOUDREADERS, an alternative trade school, and Post-Novis, an anti-disciplinary collective. Their work has been exhibited at the Chicago Architecture Biennial, International Architecture Biennale Rotterdam, Centre Pompidou, MoMA, Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Puerto Rico, and MAAT Lisbon. Garcia and Frankowski have published Universal Principles of Architecture (Rockport Publishers, 2023), A Manual of Anti-Racist Architecture Education (Loudreaders Publishers, 2021), and Narrative Architecture: A Kynical Manifesto (NAi010 Publishers, 2020), among others. WAI interrogates architectural norms through collective pedagogy, poetic critique, and radical reimaginings of the built and unbuilt world.

title.rendered: Performance: Please Don’t Flush!

content.rendered:
Please Don’t Flush!

Tuesday, September 22, 6–8 pm
303 Bond Street, Brooklyn

 

Free with RSVP

 

Presented in conjunction with NYC Climate Week 2026, Please Don’t Flush is a municipal comedy about a community board scheduled to vote on a mysterious waterfront development that neighbors and seagulls and plumbers are worried will increase inland flooding.

 

Instead, the board is derailed by planning their bi-annual gala, celebrating their second-vice-chair’s half birthday, and locking the anti-anti-anti-anti-development coalition in the bathroom.

 

Before and after the performance, stop by resource tables hosted by Van Alen Institute, Center for Urban Pedagogy (CUP), NYC Emergency Management (NYCEM), Waterfront Alliance, Fifth Avenue Committee, the Center for NYC Neighborhoods, Field Form, and more.

About

Please Don’t Flush is created by Sabina Sethi Unni, a theater director, public artist, and community organizer dedicated to telling funny stories about crumbling infrastructure (and neighbors organizing to save it). Developed in deep partnership with NYCEM and the Waterfront Alliance, the performance pairs music and laughs with resources about flooding.

Please Don’t Flush is part of the Flood Sensor Aunty extended universe, a play which toured twenty public spaces across New York City, and was covered in Grist, NY1, the CITY, and more. This performance is supported by the Waterfront Alliance, NYCEM, and the Asian Women’s Giving Circle.

Team

Written and directed by: Sabina Sethi Unni
Performers: Ray Jordan Achan, Fahad Ahmad, Amr Kotb, Amar Bains, Kshithij Hegde, Jess Balgobin, Jill Cornell, Maribelle Flint, and Josabeth Simisterra

Van Alen is delighted to host the fourth edition of PUBLIC ART PARTY, a bi-annual community-building event for people working across every part of the public art ecosystem. Artists, fabricators, public art administrators, real estate developers, private art consultants, public art curators, and more are welcomed to join this community-building event.

 

The topic will be “Future Shook,” a play on the 1970 book Future Shock by Alvin Toffler, who coined the term “as a way of describing the social paralysis induced by rapid technological change.” That change has only intensified in the past 56 years, moving faster than we can grasp or counteract. Who can blame us for feeling shook?

 

What is the future of public art as it faces these light-speed changes — not just in terms of new materials and technologies, but what we ask of public art? How will those demands expand or limit public art’s artistic possibilities? How will permanence or temporariness affect what artists decide to make, how it’s funded, and how it’s received by the public?

Jean Cooney, Executive Director, Creative Time

Shaun Leonardo, Executive Director, Socrates Sculpture Park

Mia Pearlman, Artist and Moderator

content.rendered:
Van Alen Fall Fest 2026
Saturday, October 17, 12–4 pm
303 Bond Street, Brooklyn

Free and open to the public; RSVPs are appreciated.

Join us for our annual open house to learn more about Van Alen and meet your neighbors! View our exhibition Open Access: Exploring 130 Years of American Design, which invites five artists and design teams to respond to Van Alen’s 130-year-old archive, and engage with the exhibiting artists about their work.

Then stick around to participate in all-ages art workshops and enjoy apple cider donuts and hot cider from Treelicious Orchards!

Proudly presented in collaboration with Archtober and Gowanus Open Studios.

RSVP

Workshop Schedule

12–1:30 pm: Masquerade Masks with Zofia Kostyrko

Inspired by Van Alen’s historic invitations to the Beaux Arts Ball, design your own masquerade mask as if you were attending the Ball! All ages welcome. Born in communist Warsaw, Zofia grew up surrounded by the Polish avant-garde theatre and visual arts. After moving solo to the US, she graduated from the Art Center College of Design in Pasadena, CA and built a family and a career in themed entertainment at Walt Disney Imagineering as a Senior Concept Designer. In 2000, she started her independent design studio deZign sKape LLC while developing a large body of art works held in private collections and shown in multiple exhibitions. In 2025, she joined Powerhouse Arts as a member of their ceramic arts studio and volunteer for their outreach programs.

12:30–2 pm: Gowanus Yearbook

Gowanus Yearbook is a living portrait of Gowanus. Get your photo taken, mark your photos with the year you arrived or were born in Gowanus, and draw a symbol answering the prompt: “What makes Gowanus Gowanus?” All ages welcome. Created by Rida Chaudhry, Ananaya Singh, and Kaye Yuvallos, this project is grounded in a simple but urgent idea: everyone experiences and perceives where they live differently. In neighborhoods undergoing rapid development, local histories are often at risk of being lost or diminished. Gowanus Yearbook responds to that pressure by treating memory as something communal, lived, and worth protecting.

2–3:30 pm: Collage Your City with Marcus Wilford

Using materials from Van Alen’s archive, create a collage of your vision of a resilient city! Ages 12+. Marcus Wilford is an architect, educator and urban designer based in New York, originally from Trinidad. His professional work spans public memorials, cultural buildings, and housing developments at leading design firms. Working across scales, he has contributed to exhibition designs for artists at major international museums, mixed-use urban buildings, and rural architectural projects. He is the co-founder of Modeling Community Visions for the BQE, developed in collaboration with the Institute for Public Architecture, an initiative that explores alternative models for shared urban futures and civic infrastructure.

title.rendered: Public Space as a Living Lab

content.rendered:
Public Space as a Living Lab: Scientific Protocols for Human Dynamics
Friday, October 9–Sunday, October 11, 8:30 am–5:30 pm
303 Bond Street, Brooklyn

Organized by the Academy of Neuroscience for Architecture (ANFA) and X-Topia, this three-day immersive workshop introduces architects, urban designers, planners, researchers and public-sector professionals to scientific protocols for measuring human experience in public space. Gain practical tools to design healthier, more livable, and human-centered public spaces while exploring innovative approaches at the intersection of design, science, and technology.

This workshop is co-led by Julia del Rio, Advisory Council member, ANFA; and Marcella Del Signore, Principal, X-Topia, with an international team of leading experts in urban design, environmental psychology, neuroscience, architecture, and public-space research. Together they’ll guide participants through lectures, fieldwork, experiments, and collaborative design activities across the three-day program.

Participants will work across three parallel tracks:

  • Cognition & Navigation: How do people orient themselves, remember landmarks, make decisions, and move through urban environments?
  • Mood, Stress & Restoration: How do public spaces affect emotional state, perceived restoration, stress, comfort, and attention?
  • Behavior & Social Interaction: How do spatial conditions influence dwelling, encounter, movement, seating, and collective use of public space?

Public Space as a Living Lab is open to students, professionals, researchers, and civic practitioners interested in the relationship between people and the built environment. No prior experience with neuroscience or data collection is required.

Learn more, view the full agenda, and register on Eventbrite. For additional information, contact the organizing team at info@x-topia.org.

title.rendered: NOT NOT: Closing Talk + Fire Sale

content.rendered:
NOT NOT: Closing Talk + Fire Sale

​Thursday, August 13, 6–8 pm
303 Bond Street, Brooklyn

RSVP

​Join us for a closing talk (and exhibition fire sale!) celebrating NOT NOT: An Office, An Exhibition. This summer, Van Alen has transformed into an exhibition and temporary office space of the newly-launched design studio NOT NOT. For this witty, experimental project, they created a space-within-a-space largely using off-the-shelf materials.

​To close out the exhibition, NOT NOT founders Ekin Bilal and Celia Chaussabel explore this notion: Architecture practices rarely start with a building. They often start with something smaller and scrappier: a piece of furniture, a feasibility study, a grant, a drawing set, or some oddly specific problem someone was willing to pay for. These projects may not typically be considered “architecture,” but they’re also not not architecture.

Hear from founding principals of three firms about their first “not not” commission: a paid project that sat at the edges of architecture, but somehow became part of their practice. Speakers include:

  • ​Annie Barrett, Founding Principal, aanda
  • ​Jaffer Kolb, Co-Founder and Principal, New Affiliates
  • ​Marc Tsurumaki, Principal, LTL

​Following the talk, enjoy refreshments and join in on the NOT NOT fire sale. In the exhibition’s ethos of sustainability and circular economies, select display items and building materials will be for sale. Take home a zine, print, hand clamp, or building supplies. After the close of the exhibition, all remaining building materials will be returned to their original sources.

RSVP

This event is presented by the Van Alen Vanguard, a dynamic network of emerging design leaders. Ekin Bilal and Celia Chaussabel are among the inaugural cohort developing public programs and exhibitions that reimagine designers’ roles in civic life and center equity, resilience, and local knowledge.

content.rendered:
An Evening with NOT NOT
Presented by the AIANY Committee on Residential Architecture
Tuesday, August 4, 6–7:30 pm
303 Bond Street, Brooklyn

Join AIANY’s Committee on Residential Architecture for a special summer gathering at Van Alen Institute. This event is free with RSVP and open to the public.

RSVP

The evening begins with opening remarks from Michael Landry, Project Principal, Dowbuilt and Committee Co-Chair, and Stephen Moser, Principal, Stephen Moser Architects and Committee Co-Chair.

Stephen then joins Ekin Bilal and Celia Chaussabel, founders of the emerging architecture and design practice NOT NOT, for an informal conversation about launching a young practice in New York and the ideas that shape their work.

Together, they’ll explore contemporary questions surrounding residential architecture and domesticity, from accessory dwelling units (ADUs) and alternative models of living to curiosity, invention, and play as tools for design. The discussion will also draw on workshops previously taught by Ekin and Celia, such as Chasing Dust Bunnies, which tested alternative approaches to architectural image-making by focusing on small, fragmented views of a space in order to capture architecture’s overlooked moments. It will also reference the idea of “uninhabitable space,” challenging conventional assumptions about how we inhabit, adapt, and reimagine the built environment.

The evening will conclude with refreshments, an exhibition viewing of NOT NOT: An Office, An Exhibition, and a playful interactive activity inspired by Chasing Dust Bunnies.
